plan.contextChunk: This figure stacks three waveform traces on a shared horizontal time axis to compare two ways of encoding a message on a radio carrier. The topmost trace is a smooth black curve with two broad crests separated by a single trough, labeled Signal at its right end; it is the slowly varying information waveform. Below it a red trace labeled AM oscillates far more rapidly, with the spacing between successive peaks held uniform while their height swells and shrinks: the excursion from peak to trough is largest beneath the two crests of the black curve and collapses to its smallest beneath the black trough, so the outline traced by the red peaks reproduces the shape of the signal above it. The lowest trace, drawn in blue and labeled FM, keeps a constant peak-to-trough height clear across the page while its cycles bunch tightly together below the signal crests and stretch apart below the signal trough. Setting the two carriers one beneath the other invites a direct comparison of which wave property carries the information, envelope height in one case and cycle spacing in the other. The drawing accompanies the treatment of the radio region of the electromagnetic spectrum, where amplitude modulation and frequency modulation are distinguished as the two schemes used to broadcast a signal.

interactionPlan.concept: The same slowly varying message signal can be encoded onto a fast radio carrier either by varying the carrier's amplitude (AM) or by varying its frequency (FM).
elements: Shared horizontal time axis (implicit, no tick labels) spanning the full width for all three stacked traces
Top trace: smooth black low-frequency sine-like curve with two broad crests and one central trough, labeled 'Signal' at its right end
Middle trace: red high-frequency carrier with uniform peak spacing and swelling/collapsing amplitude, labeled 'AM' at its right end
Dashed red envelope curves (upper and lower) tracing the AM peak heights, mirroring the black signal shape
Bottom trace: blue carrier with constant amplitude and varying cycle spacing — tight below signal crests, stretched below the signal trough — labeled 'FM' at its right end
Vertical time marker line crossing all three traces, with small dots at each intersection
Readout box reporting signal height, AM envelope height, and FM local cycle spacing / instantaneous frequency at the marker
Reconstructed (decoded) black curve drawn above the active carrier when decoding is enabled
Highlight/dim styling for the active vs. inactive carrier trace
Small annotation callouts: 'amplitude varies, spacing constant' on AM; 'spacing varies, amplitude constant' on FM

interactions.label: Time marker position
interactions.teaches: At any instant, the message value shows up as AM envelope height and simultaneously as FM cycle spacing — two different wave properties carrying the same number.

interactions.label: Decode carrier
interactions.teaches: Isolating one carrier and rebuilding the original signal from it shows that amplitude and frequency are interchangeable channels for the same information.

interactions.label: Show AM envelope / FM frequency track
interactions.teaches: The hidden message is made visible as the outline of the AM peaks or as the instantaneous-frequency curve of FM.

demo_steps.title: The message signal
demo_steps.narration: The black curve at the top is the slow information waveform — two crests and a trough. Everything below it is a fast radio carrier carrying this shape.

demo_steps.title: Scan the marker
demo_steps.narration: Drag the time marker across the figure. Where the black signal is high, the red AM wave is tall and the blue FM cycles crowd together; where the signal dips, AM shrinks and FM spreads out.

demo_steps.title: AM: message in the envelope
demo_steps.narration: Switch to AM. The peak spacing never changes, but the dashed envelope tracing the peak heights reproduces the original signal exactly.

demo_steps.title: FM: message in the spacing
demo_steps.narration: Switch to FM. Every cycle is the same height, yet counting cycles per unit time recovers the very same black curve.

demo_steps.title: Same message, two encodings
demo_steps.narration: Compare both decoded curves: identical information, carried by two independent properties of the wave — which is why FM survives amplitude noise that would corrupt AM.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A wave has several independent properties, and any one of them can carry a message: AM writes the signal into the carrier's height, FM writes the same signal into the carrier's cycle spacing.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Three horizontally stacked traces on a white background sharing an invisible common time axis, each labeled in black text at the right margin: 'Signal' (top, black, ~2px stroke), 'AM' (middle, brick red), 'FM' (bottom, steel blue). Top black curve is roughly one and a half slow cycles: high crest left, broad trough center, high crest right. Red AM trace has about 20 uniformly spaced cycles; amplitude is maximal under the black crests and pinches to a narrow waist under the black trough, so its peak outline copies the signal. Blue FM trace has constant amplitude throughout with cycles visibly compressed under the crests and stretched under the trough. When envelopes are on, draw dashed red mirror-image envelope curves hugging the AM peaks and a thin dashed black 'recovered signal' curve above the active carrier. A vertical gray marker line spans all three traces with small filled dots at each crossing, and a compact readout panel in a corner shows signal amplitude, AM envelope height, and FM cycle spacing at the marker. Inactive traces dim to light gray when one carrier is selected.

authoredContext:
Many valuable technologies operate in the radio (3 kHz-300 GHz) frequency region of the electromagnetic spectrum. At the low frequency (low energy, long wavelength) end of this region are AM (amplitude modulation) radio signals (540-2830 kHz) that can travel long distances. FM (frequency modulation) radio signals are used at higher frequencies (87.5-108.0 MHz). In AM radio, the information is transmitted by varying the amplitude of the wave (the figure). In FM radio, by contrast, the amplitude is constant and the instantaneous frequency varies.

This schematic depicts how amplitude modulation (AM) and frequency modulation (FM) can be used to transmit a radio wave.

This figure shows 3 wave diagrams. The first wave diagram is in black and shows two crests, indicates a consistent distance from peak to trough, and has one trough in its span across the page. The label, “Signal,” appears to the right. Just below this, a wave diagram is shown in red. The wave includes sixteen crests, but the distance from the peaks to troughs of consecutive waves varies moving across the page. The peak to trough distance is greatest in the region below the peaks of the black wave diagram, and the distance from peak to trough is similarly least below the trough of the black wave diagram. This red wave diagram is labeled, “A M.” The third wave diagram is shown in blue. The distance from peak to trough of consecutive waves is constant across the page, but the peaks and troughs are more closely packed in the region below the peaks of the black wave diagram at the top of the figure. The peaks and troughs are relatively widely spaced below the trough region of the black wave diagram. This blue wave diagram is labeled “F M.”

Other technologies also operate in the radio-wave portion of the electromagnetic spectrum. For example, 4G cellular telephone signals are approximately 880 MHz, while Global Positioning System (GPS) signals operate at 1.228 and 1.575 GHz, local area wireless technology (Wi-Fi) networks operate at 2.4 to 5 GHz, and highway toll sensors operate at 5.8 GHz. The frequencies associated with these applications are convenient because such waves tend not to be absorbed much by common building materials.

discrepancies: Stroke weights are noticeably thinner than the source, which uses heavy bold strokes for all three traces; the generated figure reads as a lighter, more delicate line plot.
The 'Signal' / 'AM' / 'FM' right-margin labels are rendered much smaller relative to the figure than in the source, where they are large and prominent.

A large empty band is reserved below the FM trace (for the marker readout box), so the three waveforms are pushed into the upper ~75% of the canvas, changing the balanced vertical composition of the source.
The FM frequency swing appears visually subtler than the source, where the crowding/stretching of the blue cycles around the signal trough is clearly pronounced.
AM cycle amplitude at the envelope maximum looks slightly reduced relative to the vertical spacing between traces compared with the source, where the red waveform is the visually dominant element.
evaluation.notes: A faithful, correctly-modelled AM/FM stack with excellent, pedagogically meaningful interactions (step player, marker slider, carrier selector, envelope/decode overlay), let down mainly by thin stroke weights, undersized trace labels, and extra reserved whitespace under the FM trace that alters the source's composition.
action_items: Increase base stroke widths (~3-4 px at default size) for the signal, AM and FM traces to match the bold look of the source.
Enlarge the 'Signal', 'AM', 'FM' labels (≈16-18 px) so they carry the same visual weight as in the source and remain legible at inline size.

Rebalance the y-range / layout so the three traces fill the canvas vertically as in the source; draw the marker readout as a floating overlay near the marker rather than reserving a permanent empty strip.
Increase the FM deviation slightly (or reduce the carrier frequency) so the cycle crowding/stretching is as visually obvious as in the source image.

feedback.rationale: Concept and interaction structure are sound (concept 5, no failure modes, empty plan action items); remaining issues are purely implementation details like stroke widths, label sizes, layout whitespace, and FM deviation tuning.

AM vertical extent/amplitude appears slightly compressed relative to the source (the source red trace spans a taller band relative to the signal and FM rows), and its waist minimum is a bit deeper/narrower in the original.

Optional overlay annotations added in later steps ('decoded (AM)', 'decoded (FM)', 'height varies', 'spacing varies') use ~8–10 px type in a narrow right margin, risking clipping and being too small to read comfortably; the source has only three large right-hand labels.
claude-opus-5.notes: Default state is a convincing drop-in replacement for the source (three stacked traces, correct colors, Signal/AM/FM labels) with a rich, genuinely pedagogical set of interactions (step player, time marker, carrier selector, envelope/decoded overlays); weaknesses are lighter stroke weights, an under-pronounced FM deviation, and very small optional overlay labels squeezed into the right margin.
action_items: Increase base stroke width for the three primary traces (and raise the minimum px floor) so they read as bold as the source at inline size.
Raise the FM deviation (e.g. DEV ≈ 6–7 with FC_FM ≈ 22) so the mid-section cycle stretching is as visually obvious as in the original.
Slightly increase AM_A (or deepen the envelope minimum toward ~0.15) so the red trace's vertical extent and waist match the source proportions.
Enlarge the optional overlay labels to at least 11–12 px and widen the right padding (or place 'decoded (AM/FM)' inside the plot band) so they cannot clip or crowd the AM/FM labels.
